parsed_answer.content: Global Exception Handling in Spring-based architectures is the practice of centralizing error logic to decouple business concerns from cross-cutting concerns like error reporting and HTTP status mapping. In a typical REST API or WebFlux microservice, allowing exceptions to bubble up to the servlet container or the Netty event loop results in inconsistent, non-standardized error responses that leak implementation details. @ControllerAdvice acts as a specialized interceptor—a component-scanned bean that uses AOP under the hood to capture exceptions thrown by any @Controller or @RestController. By centralizing this, you ensure that every 404, 400, or 500 error follows a strict, predictable JSON schema, which is vital for maintaining robust contract-first API development.

rows: Low (Business logic mixed with error handling)

items: The @ControllerAdvice annotation is a specialized @Component, meaning it is picked up by component scanning and registered as a bean in the ApplicationContext.
When an exception is thrown, the DispatcherServlet (or WebHandler in WebFlux) iterates through registered ExceptionHandlers to find the most specific match based on the exception hierarchy.
In WebFlux, @ControllerAdvice works asynchronously; the handler methods can return Mono or Flux, allowing non-blocking error transformation without stalling the event loop.
The @ExceptionHandler annotation within the advice class acts as the selector; if you define a method for 'RuntimeException.class', it will catch all subclasses unless a more specific handler exists.

parsed_answer.content: Senior Insight: Be wary of catching 'Exception.class' too broadly. If you swallow exceptions that should trigger a circuit breaker (like Hystrix or Resilience4j), you mask underlying microservice instability. Always log the full stack trace at the ERROR level before returning the sanitized response to the client; otherwise, you'll be debugging 'silent' failures in production with no visibility.
